buildUp: Start with the goal of working in human spaces, which fixes the shape: about human height, two legs to handle stairs and kerbs, two arms with hands to use the same handles and tools.

Each way a joint can turn needs its own motor, so a shoulder or hip gets three actuators, an elbow or knee one, around 30 or more in all, each with a gearbox, a brake and sensors for angle and effort.

Two legs are unstable, so a computer reads an inertial sensor and force sensors in the feet and joints and updates every motor many hundreds of times a second, with springy, softly controlled ankles making the finest corrections.

Heavy motors at the ends of limbs would make them slow and power-hungry, so the finger motors move to the forearm and pull tendon cables, and the ankle actuators sit near the knee and push through rods.
Everything is fed from a battery in the chest, where its weight sits near the centre of the body, and loads travel from hands to feet through a stiff spine and pelvis.
Finally, cameras in a head that can turn give the robot stereo vision, and AI models running on the computer turn what it sees into where its hands and feet should go.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Copy the human layout and replace muscles with electric actuators and reflexes with a fast computer. Each joint gets a motor, gearbox and sensors, and a balance controller adjusts all of them hundreds of times a second to keep the robot's weight over its feet. On top of that, cameras and AI models decide what to do, so the same body can be taught new tasks in software rather than rebuilt.

hardParts.title: Not falling over, ever
hardParts.why: The robot must stay upright while walking on uneven floors, carrying shifting loads and being bumped, and a mistake can damage it or hurt someone. The balance controller has to blend readings from many sensors, predict how the whole body will move and adjust every joint within a few thousandths of a second, while feet land at slightly different times and surfaces than expected.

hardParts.title: A hand as capable as ours
hardParts.why: A robot hand has to be slim and light, yet able both to crack an egg gently and to grip a tool firmly. A human hand packs about 27 bones, dense touch sensing and strong muscles mostly kept in the forearm into something you can wave around effortlessly. Matching even part of that means fitting more than a dozen joints, tendon cables that stretch and rub as the wrist bends, and touch sensors, into that slim, light hand.

hardParts.title: Strong, light joints that don't overheat
hardParts.why: Hips and knees must produce enough turning force to lift the whole body out of a crouch, yet stay light, quiet, efficient and tough enough for millions of steps. Motors pushed hard turn energy into heat in their windings, so the joints that work hardest, like the knees and hips during squats and stair climbing, set limits on how long and how hard the robot can work.

principles.explanation: A robot standing on two small feet is like a broom balanced on your palm: its weight sits high above a small base, so any lean grows by itself. As long as the point straight under its centre of mass stays inside the area of its feet, it can push back; once it drifts outside, it will fall unless it steps. For something about a metre tall, a lean starts running away in a few tenths of a second, which is why the controller has to sense and correct many hundreds of times a second. Walking deliberately lets the body tip forwards, then catches it with the next foot.
principles.title: Standing is balancing an upside-down pendulum

principles.explanation: A gearbox slows each joint's small, fast motor about 50 to 100 times, multiplying its turning force enough for a knee or hip to move the body slowly but strongly. Small electric motors are good at spinning fast but weak at turning hard. Power is turning force times speed, so slowing the motor down multiplies its turning force by nearly the same amount, minus some friction. Holding a 70 kg body with a bent knee needs on the order of a hundred newton-metres at that joint, like hanging a 10 kg weight on the end of a metre-long bar. Too much gearing makes a joint stiff and hard to push back, so designers balance strength against the ability to feel and give way.
principles.title: Gearboxes trade speed for force

principles.explanation: Weight costs far more the further it sits from a joint, so designers put the heavy motors close to the body and send their force out along the limbs. How hard a limb is to swing depends on its mass times the square of its distance from the joint, so a kilogram at the hand costs far more than a kilogram near the shoulder. That is why a hammer swings easily held by its head and hard held by its handle's end. Every gram at the end of a limb also needs bigger motors further up to move it, which need more battery, which needs stronger legs. So the heavy motors sit in the forearm and near the knee, and the force goes out through cables and push rods.
principles.title: Weight far from a joint is expensive

principles.explanation: The battery holds about as much energy as a person's food for a day, yet the robot drains it in only a few hours. A battery of about 2 to 2.5 kWh holds roughly the energy in a day's food for a person, about 2,000 kilocalories. But the robot spends it much faster: walking takes several hundred watts, the computer about 100 W more, so it lasts a few hours. Muscles are also cheap at holding still, while an electric motor holding a load against gravity uses power the whole time, which is one reason joints have brakes. Every part of the design, from light hollow links to efficient gears, is shaped by how far that battery has to go.
principles.title: The energy budget is tight

firstPrinciples.problem: Build one machine that can do many different jobs in places made for people: walk through doorways, climb stairs, open drawers, carry boxes and use ordinary tools, without the building being changed for it. Wheels are simpler and more stable but stop at a step, and a specialised machine does one job well but nothing else. Two legs and two hands can go almost anywhere a person can, but they are naturally unstable, need dozens of strong yet light joints, and have to be powered by a battery the robot carries itself.

questions.answer: Feet apart make a bigger area for its centre of mass to stay above, so it can lean further before it starts to tip. With feet together that area is tiny, and the controller has to make much quicker, bigger corrections.
questions.question: Why is it easier for a humanoid robot to stand still with its feet apart than with them together?

questions.answer: Mass at the end of a limb is very costly to move, because it acts far from the shoulder and elbow. Moving the motors into the forearm keeps the hand light and slim, and the cables carry their pull out to the fingers, much like the tendons in your own arm.
questions.question: Why are the finger motors in the forearm rather than in the fingers themselves?

questions.answer: Each camera sees the cup from a slightly different position, so it appears shifted between the two images. The closer the cup, the bigger the shift, and the computer converts that shift into a distance, just as your two eyes do.
questions.question: How can two cameras in the head tell how far away a cup is?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The hardware alone, motors, gears and a battery, has existed for decades; what makes today's humanoids work is software that turns it into reflexes and skills. Fast balance control lets the body treat walking as a controlled fall, and AI models trained on huge amounts of experience let a robot recognise objects and work out how to handle them, so one general body can be given new jobs by changing its software rather than its parts.

name: Humanoid Robot
overview:
A humanoid robot is built in our shape so it can work in places designed for people: climb stairs, open doors, carry boxes, use the same tools. Underneath the smooth covers it is a skeleton of metal links joined by around 30 or more actuators, each a compact electric motor with a gearbox, a brake and sensors that measure its angle and how hard it is pushing. A shoulder or hip needs a few of these, one for each direction it can turn.

Standing up is a constant balancing act. A computer in the torso reads an inertial sensor, like the one in your inner ear, plus force sensors in the feet and joints hundreds of times a second, and adjusts every motor to keep the robot's weight over its feet. Walking is really a controlled fall from one foot to the other.

The hands are the hardest part. To fit a human-sized hand with more than a dozen joints, the motors usually sit in the forearm and pull the fingers through cables, like the tendons in your own arm. Cameras in the head feed an AI model that recognises objects and decides how to move, and a battery pack in the chest gives a few hours of work before it has to recharge.

parts.description: Smooth shell over the head's cameras and electronics; there's no face, just a dark visor.

details.didYouKnow: Many humanoids avoid a realistic face on purpose. In 1970 the Japanese roboticist Masahiro Mori described the 'uncanny valley', the uneasy feeling people get from machines that look almost, but not quite, human.
details.howItWorks: The head shell is a lightweight cover clipped over a small internal frame that holds the cameras, and often microphones, a speaker and status lights. It sits on top of the neck actuator, so the less it weighs the faster and more precisely the neck can point it. Its rounded, featureless shape is deliberate: it is easy to clean, has nothing to snag, and gives people a clear sense of which way the robot is facing.
keyNumbers: Typically about 20 to 25 cm tall
Usually only a few kilograms including cameras
Sits roughly 1.5 to 1.7 m off the ground
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded engineering plastic such as polycarbonate or a polycarbonate blend, painted or textured on the outside. Plastic is light, tough enough to survive a fall, and does not block the radio signals from wireless antennas inside.

parts.name: Head shell

parts.description: Dark glossy panel across the front of the head that the cameras look out through.

details.didYouKnow: A tinted visor works like one-way glass: because the inside of the head is darker than the room, people see a black mirror while the cameras behind it still get a clear view.
details.howItWorks: The visor is a window: the cameras and other sensors sit just behind it and look out through the dark glossy surface. Because the tint hides what is inside, the robot looks calm and uniform while the lenses are protected from dust, knocks and fingerprints. On some designs lights or a simple display behind the visor show the robot's status, such as when it is listening or working.
keyNumbers: Typically about 15 cm wide
A few millimetres thick
Lets through enough light for cameras typically running at about 30 to 60 frames per second
details.madeOf: Tinted polycarbonate or toughened glass with an anti-scratch and anti-reflection coating. The material has to stay optically clear for the cameras while being dark enough to hide them from outside.

parts.name: Face visor

parts.description: Pair of cameras set apart like eyes, so the robot can judge depth; more cameras round the body fill in the view.

details.didYouKnow: Stereo depth gets worse quickly with distance: doubling how far away something is makes the depth error roughly four times bigger, which is why robots, like people, judge depth best within arm's reach.
details.howItWorks: Two cameras a few centimetres apart see the same scene from slightly different angles, and the computer measures how far each object shifts between the two images to work out its distance, just as your brain does with your eyes. The images stream to the AI computer in the chest, where neural networks pick out objects, people, hands and surfaces. Extra cameras on the body cover the sides, the back and the hands' working area so there are fewer blind spots.
keyNumbers: Cameras typically about 6 to 10 cm apart, similar to human eyes at about 6.3 cm
Often several cameras round the body in total
Each frame reaches the computer in a few hundredths of a second
details.madeOf: Small silicon image sensors behind stacks of moulded glass or plastic lenses, mounted on a rigid bracket. The bracket must not flex, because even a tiny shift between the two cameras would spoil the depth estimates.

parts.name: Head cameras

parts.description: Actuator that turns and tilts the head to look around.

details.didYouKnow: The human head weighs about 8 percent of the body, roughly 5 kg for an adult, which is why people's necks need strong muscles and a robot's, with its lighter head, can manage with small motors.
details.howItWorks: The neck usually has two or three small rotary actuators: one to turn the head left and right, one to nod it up and down, and sometimes one to tilt it. Pointing the head lets the cameras look at the hands while working, or check the floor before a step. The control software also uses the neck to keep the cameras steady while the body sways, much as your eyes stay fixed on something while you walk.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 to 3 degrees of freedom
Turns the head roughly 70 to 90 degrees each way
Carries a head of only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Compact electric motors with small gearboxes in cast or machined aluminium housings. These are among the smallest actuators in the body because the head is light.

parts.name: Neck actuator

parts.description: Front body panel of tough plastic that protects the battery and computer and gives the robot its shape.

details.didYouKnow: Smooth body covers are partly a safety feature: by hiding the gaps between moving joints, they stop people from getting fingers pinched when they work alongside the robot.
details.howItWorks: The chest cover is a shell that clips or screws onto the spine frame and carries almost no load itself. Its job is to protect the battery and computer from knocks, keep fingers and loose clothing away from moving parts and give the robot a smooth, friendly shape. It comes off quickly so technicians can reach the battery and electronics.
keyNumbers: Typically a few millimetres thick
Weighs roughly 1 kg or less
Covers a torso roughly 40 cm wide
details.madeOf: Tough moulded plastic such as polycarbonate, ABS or nylon, sometimes with a soft-touch finish. Plastic dents less than thin metal when bumped, is cheap to shape and lets wireless signals through.

parts.name: Chest cover

parts.description: Rear body panel with cooling vents for the computer and battery.

details.didYouKnow: Your body uses its skin and sweat to shed the 100 or so watts it makes at rest; a working humanoid can need to shed several times that, mostly from its motors and computer.
details.howItWorks: The back cover closes up the rear of the torso and carries the vents that let fans pull cool air across the computer, battery and power electronics and push warm air out. Keeping things cool matters because both chips and lithium-ion cells slow down or age faster when hot. It is often also where the charging port, emergency stop or service connectors are reached.
keyNumbers: Electronics usually kept below about 60 to 80 degrees C
Computer and drives together can produce hundreds of watts of heat
Fans typically a few centimetres across
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic like the chest cover, with vent slots and filters moulded in. Plastic keeps the panel light and stops it getting hot to the touch.

parts.name: Back cover

parts.description: Aluminium backbone that everything bolts to, carrying loads from the arms and head down to the hips.

details.didYouKnow: Your spine has 33 vertebrae and bends in many places, but most humanoid torsos are a single rigid frame with just one waist joint, which makes balance control simpler.
details.howItWorks: The spine frame is the robot's main structure, a stiff metal backbone that the shoulders, neck, battery, computer and covers all bolt onto. Every time the robot lifts a box, the load travels from the hands through the arms and shoulders into this frame, then down through the waist into the pelvis and legs. It also carries the main cable runs and power lines between the upper and lower body.
keyNumbers: Typically about 40 to 50 cm long
Carries the whole upper body of roughly 25 to 40 kg plus any payload
Payloads typically up to about 20 kg
details.madeOf: Machined or cast aluminium alloy, sometimes with carbon fibre parts. Aluminium gives a good balance of stiffness, low weight and easy machining, and it also helps spread heat from mounted electronics.

parts.name: Spine frame

parts.description: Lithium-ion pack in the chest, where its weight sits close to the robot's centre of balance.

details.didYouKnow: A pack of about 2.3 kWh holds roughly the same energy as 2,000 food calories, close to what an adult eats in a day, yet the robot uses it up in a few hours.
details.howItWorks: The pack holds many lithium-ion cells wired together to give a high voltage, which feeds power converters that supply every actuator and the computer. A battery management system watches each cell's voltage and temperature, balances them and can cut the power if anything goes wrong. When the robot slows down or lowers a load, some actuators can briefly push energy back into the pack.
keyNumbers: About 2 to 2.5 kWh of energy
Roughly 10 to 15 kg
Typically a few hours of work per charge
Draws several hundred watts while walking
details.madeOf: Cylindrical or pouch lithium-ion cells in an aluminium case with cooling plates and a circuit board for monitoring. Aluminium is light, strong enough to protect the cells in a fall and good at carrying heat away.

parts.name: Battery pack

parts.description: Onboard computer that runs the balance control and the AI model that turns what the cameras see into movements.

details.didYouKnow: Much of what the AI knows comes from practice in simulation, where thousands of virtual robots can learn to walk at once and gather years of experience in a few hours, plus recordings of people demonstrating tasks.
details.howItWorks: The computer runs several layers of software at once. A fast balance loop reads the inertial sensor, foot sensors and joint sensors and updates every motor command hundreds to about a thousand times a second. On top of that, AI models turn camera images into an understanding of the scene and decide where the hands and feet should go, running more slowly but feeding targets to the balance layer.
keyNumbers: Balance control typically about 500 to 1,000 updates per second
Can draw roughly 100 W or more
Human reaction time is about 0.2 seconds, far slower than the balance loop
details.madeOf: Processor chips with graphics-style AI accelerators on circuit boards, under a metal heat sink with fans. These are similar to the chips used in self-driving cars, chosen because they run neural networks quickly on battery power.

parts.name: AI computer

parts.description: Inertial sensor near the centre of the body that feels tilt and acceleration, like the balance organ in your inner ear.

details.didYouKnow: A chip like this drifts: left alone its idea of 'up' slowly wanders, so robots constantly correct it using gravity, which is the same reference your inner ear relies on.
details.howItWorks: Tiny vibrating structures on a chip feel acceleration and rotation in all three directions, hundreds or thousands of times a second. The computer combines those readings with what the joints and feet report to work out which way is up and how fast the body is tipping.
keyNumbers: Typically 6 axes: 3 of acceleration, 3 of rotation
Often read hundreds to thousands of times a second
About the size of a matchbox with its case
details.madeOf: A MEMS silicon sensor chip on a small circuit board, in a stiff aluminium case bolted close to the robot's centre so it measures the body rather than a vibrating limb.

parts.name: Balance sensor

parts.description: Board that feeds battery power out to every limb and can cut it instantly if the robot needs to stop.

details.didYouKnow: Higher voltage is a weight saving: for the same power, doubling the voltage halves the current, so a robot can use thinner, lighter cables throughout its body.
details.howItWorks: Battery current arrives on thick copper bars and is split into protected branches for each limb, the computer and the sensors. Power switches can disconnect the motors within milliseconds when the emergency stop fires or a fault is detected.
keyNumbers: Often carries tens to hundreds of amps at peak
Battery voltage typically several tens of volts or more
Faults are typically cut off within milliseconds
details.madeOf: A thick-copper circuit board with high-current transistors, fuses and connectors. The copper layers are much heavier than on a normal board because they carry tens of amps or more.

parts.name: Power board

parts.description: Actuator that twists the upper body on the hips, so it can turn to a shelf without moving its feet.

details.didYouKnow: Some newer humanoids can turn their waist far beyond a human's range, letting the robot swivel its whole upper body round to face backwards without moving its feet.
details.howItWorks: The waist actuator sits between the spine frame and the pelvis and rotates the whole upper body. Turning at the waist is quicker and safer than shuffling the feet, and it lets the robot pass an object from one side to the other while staying planted. The balance controller also uses it to counter the twisting forces from swinging arms and legs.
keyNumbers: Usually 1 to 3 degrees of freedom
Carries roughly half the robot's weight above it
Humans twist the trunk only about 30 to 45 degrees each way
details.madeOf: An electric motor with a strain-wave or planetary gearbox in a cast aluminium housing, plus a large bearing to take the weight above it. The bearing has to handle the bending load from the upper body, not just the twist.

parts.name: Waist actuator

parts.description: Pleated rubber sleeve that closes the gap between chest and hips while still letting the waist bend and twist.

details.didYouKnow: The same concertina shape protects car driveshaft joints and the gear levers of old cars: it is the simplest way to seal something that has to keep moving.
details.howItWorks: Each pleat opens on the outside of a bend and closes on the inside, so the sleeve changes shape without stretching much. That keeps dust and fingers out of the waist actuator through its whole range of motion.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 20 pleats on a sleeve this size
Wall usually only a millimetre or two thick
Must survive many thousands of bends
details.madeOf: Moulded synthetic rubber such as silicone or EPDM, picked because it stays flexible over many bends and across a wide temperature range.

parts.name: Waist bellows

parts.description: Strong frame at the hips that carries the whole upper body and holds the hip actuators.

details.didYouKnow: In robots and people alike, the centre of mass sits roughly at the level of the pelvis, about 55 percent of standing height, which is why balance is easiest to control from the hips.
details.howItWorks: The pelvis is the junction between the upper body and the legs. The waist actuator sits on top, and the two hip actuator groups hang off each side. Every step sends the full weight of the robot, plus impacts from landing, up through the legs into this frame, so it is one of the stiffest parts in the body. Many designs also put the inertial sensor near here, close to the centre of mass.
keyNumbers: Carries the whole body, roughly 55 to 90 kg plus payload
Landing forces can briefly reach about twice body weight
Hip joints typically about 20 cm apart
details.madeOf: Cast or machined aluminium alloy, sometimes with steel inserts where bolts and bearings carry high loads. A stiff, light pelvis helps the controller, because a frame that flexes makes the robot's position harder to predict.

parts.name: Pelvis

parts.description: Moulded cover over the front of the pelvis that keeps dirt out of the hip joints and tidies the body's outline.

details.didYouKnow: Covers on robots do double duty: as well as protecting the joints they are the parts people actually bump into, so rounded plastic is much safer around people than bare metal.
details.howItWorks: The cover clips to the pelvis frame and carries no load. It keeps grit and fingers out of the hip joints, while its shape is cut away enough that the legs can swing fully forward and back.
keyNumbers: Typically a few millimetres thick
Weighs a few hundred grams
Carries none of the body's weight
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded engineering plastic such as polycarbonate or nylon, chosen because it is light, shrugs off knocks and is cheap to replace.

parts.name: Hip cover

parts.description: Domed cover over the shoulder joint that shields the actuators and rounds off the robot's silhouette.

details.didYouKnow: Shoulders are among the most likely parts of a humanoid to hit something when it falls, so caps are designed to be cheap to replace.
details.howItWorks: The cap clips over the outer shoulder actuator and turns with it. It protects the joint from knocks, and rounding the corner here lets the arm brush past door frames and people without catching.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 20 cm across
Weighs a few hundred grams
Carries no structural load
details.madeOf: Moulded engineering plastic such as polycarbonate, with slots that let heat from the actuator beneath escape.

parts.name: Left shoulder cap

parts.description: Cluster of actuators that swing the left arm forwards, out to the side and round.

details.didYouKnow: The human shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, and also the one that dislocates most often; robot shoulders trade a little of that range for actuators that cannot pop out.
details.howItWorks: The shoulder is usually built from three rotary actuators stacked at right angles, each adding one way to turn: lifting the arm forwards, raising it out to the side and rotating it about its own length. Together they can point the upper arm almost anywhere a person's can. Software coordinates all three at once, so a reach that looks like one smooth motion is really three motors working together.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 degrees of freedom
Gear ratios commonly about 30:1 to 100:1 or more
Lifts an arm of roughly 4 to 6 kg plus anything in the hand
details.madeOf: Electric motors with strain-wave or planetary gearboxes in cast aluminium housings, each with an angle sensor and often a brake. Aluminium housings keep weight down while holding the gears and bearings precisely aligned.

parts.name: Left shoulder actuators

parts.description: Hollow structural link between shoulder and elbow, with motor cables running inside.

details.didYouKnow: Every gram in the arm counts twice: it has to be lifted by the shoulder and it also adds to the turning effort of every fast swing, so arm parts are among the most weight-optimised in the robot.
details.howItWorks: The upper arm is a hollow link that holds the shoulder and elbow actuators the right distance apart. Power and data cables for the elbow, forearm and hand motors run through its middle, protected from pinching. Its length sets how far the robot can reach, and its stiffness affects how accurately the hand ends up where the computer intended.
keyNumbers: Typically about 25 to 30 cm long
Weighs roughly 1 kg or less
Carries cables for a dozen or more motors further down the arm
details.madeOf: A structural core of aluminium or carbon fibre under a moulded plastic cover. A hollow tube shape gives a lot of stiffness for very little weight, the same reason bicycle frames are tubes.

parts.name: Left upper arm

parts.description: Carbon-fibre tube inside the upper arm shell that really carries the load, with the arm's cables taped along it.

details.didYouKnow: Light arms pay back twice: every gram near the hand also reduces the load on the elbow, the shoulder, the waist and the legs that have to balance it.
details.howItWorks: This tube is the real upper arm: it transfers the load from the elbow to the shoulder, while the white shell around it is mostly protection. Cables pass along it on their way to the elbow, wrist and hand.
keyNumbers: Typically about 25 cm long
Weighs a few hundred grams
Carbon fibre can be about as stiff as steel at a fraction of the weight
details.madeOf: A carbon-fibre tube with bonded aluminium end fittings. A hollow tube puts material far from the centre, where it does the most to resist bending, for very little weight.

parts.name: Left upper arm bone

parts.description: Rotary actuator that bends the left elbow, strong enough to lift a heavy box.

details.didYouKnow: Strain-wave gearing was invented in the 1950s and was used in the wheels of the Apollo lunar rover; today it is in almost every precise robot arm because it has almost no slack.
details.howItWorks: The elbow is a rotary actuator: a fast electric motor drives a strain-wave gearbox that slows the motion down and multiplies the turning force many times. A flexible toothed ring inside the gearbox is squeezed into an oval by a spinning cam, so its teeth walk round a fixed ring a little at a time. Sensors on both sides measure the joint angle precisely, and some designs also sense the torque so the arm can feel unexpected contact.
keyNumbers: Usually 1 degree of freedom, sometimes with a separate forearm twist
Strain-wave gear ratios typically about 50:1 to 160:1
Bends through roughly 140 degrees, like a human elbow
details.madeOf: A brushless motor, a steel strain-wave gear set and bearings in a cast aluminium housing. The steel flexing ring has to bend millions of times without cracking, so it is made from very high-quality alloy.

parts.name: Left elbow actuator

parts.description: Forearm packed with the small motors that pull the fingers through cables, keeping the hand light.

details.didYouKnow: This is exactly how your own hand works: most of the muscles that bend your fingers sit in your forearm, which you can feel moving if you hold your arm while wiggling your fingers.
details.howItWorks: The forearm holds a row of small motors, often a dozen or so, each winding a thin cable that runs through the wrist to a finger joint. Putting the motors here keeps the hand light and slim, and leaves room in the forearm for the wrist actuators as well. Sensors measure how far each cable has moved, so the computer knows how the fingers are bent even though the motors are far away.
keyNumbers: Often about 10 to 15 small motors
Hand and wrist together give roughly 11 or more degrees of freedom
Forearm typically about 25 cm long
details.madeOf: Small brushless or coreless motors with tiny gearboxes or lead screws, mounted on an aluminium or plastic frame inside a plastic shell. Lightweight plastics keep the forearm easy to swing.

parts.name: Left forearm & hand motors

parts.description: Six small motors in the forearm, each winding a steel cable that runs through the wrist to curl one finger.

details.didYouKnow: This is exactly how your own hand is built: the main muscles that bend your fingers are in your forearm, and there are no muscles in the fingers themselves.
details.howItWorks: Each small motor winds a thin steel cable. The cable runs through the wrist to one finger and curls it when pulled, much as tendons in your forearm move your fingers.
keyNumbers: Typically one motor per finger joint group
Each motor only a couple of centimetres across
Hands usually have around 10 or more joints
details.madeOf: Small brushless or coreless motors with miniature gearboxes in an aluminium carrier, driving braided steel cables.

parts.name: Left finger motors

parts.description: Palm with touch sensors and a thumb that can oppose the fingers to pinch and grip.

details.didYouKnow: Doctors often rate the thumb as about 40 percent of the whole hand's usefulness, which is why robot designers spend so much effort getting it to swing across the palm properly.
details.howItWorks: The palm anchors the fingers and the thumb, and guides the tendon cables coming from the forearm through small channels and pulleys. The thumb sits on its own base joint so it can swing across to meet the fingertips, making pinches, power grips and tool holds possible. Touch sensors in the palm and fingertips tell the computer when contact is made and roughly how hard it is pressing.
keyNumbers: Roughly human-hand sized, about 18 to 20 cm long
Typically holds a few kilograms in one hand
An adult human hand has 27 bones
details.madeOf: A plastic or aluminium palm frame with soft rubber or silicone pads over the gripping areas. The soft pads add friction and let the surface mould round an object, making grips more secure without squeezing harder.

parts.name: Left hand

parts.description: Four jointed fingers, each curled by a tendon cable and straightened by a spring or second cable.

details.didYouKnow: Using one cable to curl several joints means a finger can automatically wrap round odd shapes: when the first segment touches something and stops, the pull carries on curling the next one.
details.howItWorks: Each finger has two or three hinged segments. A tendon cable runs along the palm side, so when the forearm motor pulls it, the finger curls; a spring or a second cable on the back side straightens it again. The cable route over small pulleys at each joint decides how the curl is shared between the segments, so a single pull can wrap the finger round an object.
keyNumbers: Four fingers, typically 2 to 3 joints each
Each finger usually has 1 to 2 driving motors
Finger closing time typically under about 1 second
details.madeOf: Plastic or aluminium segments with steel or high-strength polymer fibre tendons and soft fingertip pads. Polymer fibre cables are very strong for their weight and flexible enough to bend round tight pulleys.

parts.name: Left fingers

parts.description: Group of powerful actuators that swing, spread and twist the left leg.

details.didYouKnow: Walking is really a controlled fall: with each step the hips tip the body forwards and swing a leg out just in time to catch it.
details.howItWorks: The hip has three actuators: one swings the leg forwards and back, one lifts it out to the side and one twists it to point the foot. The forward swing works hardest, pushing the body up stairs and out of a crouch, so it is usually the most powerful actuator in the robot. The side-to-side actuator does a quieter but vital job, shifting weight over the standing foot with every step.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 degrees of freedom per hip
Among the 28 or more actuators in the body, these are some of the strongest
Walking speeds typically up to roughly 1 to 2.5 m/s
details.madeOf: Large brushless motors with planetary or strain-wave gearboxes, or on some designs screw-driven linear actuators, in cast aluminium housings. They have to be strong yet light, since they are part of the leg the other hip must swing.

parts.name: Left hip actuators

parts.description: Ring of copper coils fixed inside the housing; switching current through them makes a magnetic field that spins the rotor.

details.didYouKnow: Holding still costs energy: unlike your bones locking a knee, a motor holding up weight must keep current flowing, so simply standing warms a humanoid's joints.
details.howItWorks: Electronics switch current through the coils in sequence, making a magnetic field that travels round the ring. The rotor's magnets are dragged round after it, which is what turns electricity into motion.
keyNumbers: Typically several centimetres to over 10 cm across
Copper losses heat the housing, hence the cooling fins
The left hip uses the same design as the other actuators, scaled up
details.madeOf: Copper windings on a stack of thin steel laminations. Thin insulated layers reduce the wasted currents that a solid steel core would allow.

parts.name: Left hip motor windings

parts.description: Spinning core ringed with strong magnets of alternating poles; it turns thousands of times a minute.

details.didYouKnow: Neodymium magnets lose strength if they get too hot, which is one reason robot joints have temperature sensors and reduce power when they warm up.
details.howItWorks: The rotor carries magnets of alternating north and south poles. Attracted and repelled by the rotating field in the windings, it spins at high speed, turning the input of the gearbox.
keyNumbers: Often spins at thousands of revolutions a minute
Magnets typically a few millimetres thick
Many pole pairs give smooth, strong torque
details.madeOf: A steel core ringed by rare-earth permanent magnets, usually neodymium-iron-boron, the strongest commonly available type.

parts.name: Left hip motor rotor

parts.description: Gearbox that trades the motor's speed for force: a thin flexing toothed cup walks round a slightly larger ring, about a hundred motor turns for each output turn.

details.didYouKnow: Strain-wave gears were invented in the 1950s by C. Walton Musser and flew on the Apollo lunar rover's wheel drives; the same idea now moves robot arms and humanoids.
details.howItWorks: An oval cam stretches a thin toothed cup so it meshes with a slightly larger ring at two points. The ring has a couple more teeth, so each spin of the cam shifts the cup by only a tooth or two, giving a large reduction in very little space.
keyNumbers: Reductions typically about 50:1 to 160:1
Almost no free play between the teeth
Fits inside a joint only several centimetres across
details.madeOf: A flexible cup of special alloy steel, a rigid steel ring and a precision bearing. Making metal flex billions of times without cracking takes careful material and tooth design.

parts.name: Left hip strain-wave gear

parts.description: Long, stiff thigh link built to carry the robot's weight with every step.

details.didYouKnow: In humans the thigh bone, the femur, is the longest and strongest bone in the body, at roughly a quarter of a person's height.
details.howItWorks: The thigh link connects the hip and knee and carries the robot's full weight every time this leg is on the ground. It must be stiff, because any bending changes where the foot lands. Cables for the knee and ankle run along it, and on robots with linear knee actuators the screw and motor are often tucked along the thigh itself.
keyNumbers: Typically about 35 to 45 cm long
Carries roughly the whole body weight of 55 to 90 kg on each step
Impact forces can briefly reach about 2 times body weight
details.madeOf: A machined aluminium or composite structure under a moulded plastic cover. Stiffness matters more than raw strength here, and aluminium and carbon fibre give a lot of stiffness per kilogram.

parts.name: Left thigh

parts.description: Carbon-fibre tube that takes the body's weight down the leg, with power and data cables running along it.

details.didYouKnow: Your own femur is also a hollow tube, thickest at the outside, for the same reason: most of the strength against bending comes from material far from the centre.
details.howItWorks: The tube carries the weight of the body from the hip to the knee and resists the bending that comes with every step. The shell around it adds protection and shape rather than strength.
keyNumbers: Typically about 35 to 40 cm long
Often weighs well under 1 kg
Sees several times body weight in a hard landing
details.madeOf: A carbon-fibre tube with bonded aluminium end fittings, wound so the fibres line up with the bending and twisting loads.

parts.name: Left thigh bone

parts.description: Threaded rod turned by a motor so a nut runs along it, pushing the shin like a muscle; this is what makes the knee so strong.

details.didYouKnow: Using a straight push for the knee mirrors a real leg, where the thigh muscle pulls in a line. The leverage changes with the knee angle, giving most force when deeply bent, right when climbing or rising needs it.
details.howItWorks: A motor turns the screw and a nut riding on it moves in a straight line, pushing the shin around the knee. Balls rolling in the thread keep friction low, so most of the motor's power reaches the joint.
keyNumbers: Stroke typically 10 to 15 cm
Can deliver thousands of newtons of push
Efficiency often above 80 percent
details.madeOf: A hardened steel threaded rod with a planetary-roller or ball nut in an aluminium body, with an orange-marked seal keeping grit out of the thread.

parts.name: Left knee push screw

parts.description: The robot's strongest joint, driven by a linear actuator, a screw that pushes like a muscle.

details.didYouKnow: In a roller screw, the load is carried by several small threaded rollers between the screw and nut instead of balls, spreading the force over many contact lines so it can push harder for its size.
details.howItWorks: A motor spins a roller screw or ball screw, which pushes a nut along it, so rotation becomes a straight push. That push acts on a lever at the knee and bends or straightens the joint, much like a thigh muscle pulling on the kneecap. Because the lever changes with knee angle, designers can arrange the strongest push where it is needed most, such as when the knee is bent deep to stand up.
keyNumbers: Roller screws typically turn about 90 percent of motor power into push
Usually 1 degree of freedom
Knee bends roughly 120 to 140 degrees
details.madeOf: A brushless motor, a hardened steel roller or ball screw and an aluminium housing with pivoting end mounts. Steel threads and rolling elements are needed to carry very high forces with little friction or wear.

parts.name: Left knee actuator

parts.description: Lower leg link carrying the ankle actuators' push rods down to the foot.

details.didYouKnow: Your calf muscles work the same way: they sit high on the leg and pull on the foot through the Achilles tendon, the thickest and strongest tendon in your body.
details.howItWorks: The shin connects the knee to the ankle and carries the push rods from the ankle actuators, which are usually mounted up near the knee rather than at the ankle itself. Moving that motor weight up the leg means less mass swinging at the end of each stride, so the hip and knee have an easier job. The rods pass the actuators' pull and push down to the foot like the tendons at the back of your heel.

Usually carries 2 push rods to the ankle
Takes the full body weight on every step
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite tubes under a plastic cover, with steel push rods and ball joints. The cover protects the rods and cables from knocks and stops anything getting caught.

parts.name: Left shin

parts.description: Two steel rods that carry force from motors high in the shin down to the ankle, keeping weight away from the foot so the leg swings easily.

details.didYouKnow: Mass low on the leg is expensive because it is swung with every step, and that's why runners' calves taper to thin tendons at the ankle, the same design as here.
details.howItWorks: Motors mounted high in the shin push and pull these two rods. Moving them together tips the foot up and down; moving them opposite ways rocks it from side to side, so two motors share both jobs.
keyNumbers: Typically 25 to 30 cm long
Two degrees of freedom from two rods
Ankles commonly see more than body weight on each step
details.madeOf: Steel or titanium rods with ball joints at each end, and the motors kept far above the ankle.

parts.name: Left ankle push rods

parts.description: Pair of actuators that tip the foot up, down and sideways to keep balance on uneven ground.

details.didYouKnow: Standing still, both people and robots sway gently and correct mainly at the ankles; balance scientists call it the 'ankle strategy', and switch to hip movements only for bigger pushes.
details.howItWorks: Two actuators work as a pair: when both push rods move the same way, the foot tips up or down; when they move in opposite directions, the foot rolls side to side. Sharing the load between two actuators this way means each can be smaller. The ankle is the robot's finest balance tool, making small, quick corrections to keep the weight centred over the foot before the hips need to get involved.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 degrees of freedom
Tips the foot roughly 30 to 45 degrees up and down
Corrections made hundreds of times per second

parts.name: Left ankle actuators

parts.description: Flat foot with force sensors in the sole that feel where the robot's weight is pressing.

details.didYouKnow: Keeping the pressure point under the foot is the idea behind 'zero-moment-point' walking, worked out by the Serbian scientist Miomir Vukobratovic around 1970 and used by many walking robots since, including Honda's ASIMO in 2000.
details.howItWorks: The foot spreads the robot's weight over the ground and measures exactly where that weight is pressing. Force sensors in the sole or a force and torque sensor at the ankle feed the balance controller, which keeps the pressure point inside the area of the foot. If it drifts to the edge, the robot starts to tip, so the controller shifts its body or takes a step.
keyNumbers: Typically about 20 to 25 cm long
Takes up to roughly the whole body weight on each step
Sensors read hundreds to about a thousand times per second
details.madeOf: A rigid aluminium or composite plate with force sensors, covered by a grippy rubber sole. The rubber gives grip and absorbs some of the shock of landing.

parts.name: Left foot

parts.description: Domed cover over the shoulder joint that shields the actuators and rounds off the robot's silhouette.

details.didYouKnow: Shoulders are among the most likely parts of a humanoid to hit something when it falls, so caps are designed to be cheap to replace.
details.howItWorks: The cap clips over the outer shoulder actuator and turns with it. It protects the joint from knocks, and rounding the corner here lets the arm brush past door frames and people without catching.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 20 cm across
Weighs a few hundred grams
Carries no structural load
details.madeOf: Moulded engineering plastic such as polycarbonate, with slots that let heat from the actuator beneath escape.

parts.name: Right shoulder cap

parts.description: Cluster of actuators that swing the right arm forwards, out to the side and round.

details.didYouKnow: Holding a box at arm's length is much harder for a shoulder than holding it close, because the turning effort grows with distance; that is why robots, like people, hug heavy loads to their chest.
details.howItWorks: Each of the shoulder actuators contains a brake that clamps on when power is cut, so the arm does not drop if the robot switches off. The actuators also report how hard they are working; if the effort suddenly rises without reason, such as when the arm bumps into a person, the controller can stop or go limp. This is what lets a humanoid work closer to people than a traditional caged factory robot.

Arms typically reach roughly 60 to 70 cm from shoulder to hand
Each arm commonly carries several kilograms at full stretch
details.madeOf: Electric motors, gearboxes, spring-loaded brakes and angle sensors packed into cast aluminium housings. Spring brakes are fail-safe: they grip by default and need power to release.

parts.name: Right shoulder actuators

parts.description: Hollow structural link between shoulder and elbow, with motor cables running inside.

details.didYouKnow: Worn-out cables at moving joints are one of the commonest failures in robot arms, which is why designers sometimes route signals over a single fast data line instead of many separate wires.
details.howItWorks: Running cables through a joint that turns is tricky, so the upper arm's hollow centre and generous bends let wires twist and flex without rubbing. Each cable must survive millions of bends over the robot's life. The upper arm also provides a place to mount position and temperature sensors for the elbow below.
keyNumbers: Typically about 25 to 30 cm long
Cables may need to survive millions of bend cycles
Weighs roughly 1 kg or less
details.madeOf: A plastic shell over an aluminium or carbon fibre core, with flexible, high-flex-life cabling inside. High-flex cables use many very fine copper strands so they can bend repeatedly without breaking.

parts.name: Right upper arm

parts.description: Carbon-fibre tube inside the upper arm shell that really carries the load, with the arm's cables taped along it.

details.didYouKnow: Light arms pay back twice: every gram near the hand also reduces the load on the elbow, the shoulder, the waist and the legs that have to balance it.

keyNumbers: Typically about 25 cm long
Weighs a few hundred grams
Carbon fibre can be about as stiff as steel at a fraction of the weight
details.madeOf: A carbon-fibre tube with bonded aluminium end fittings. A hollow tube puts material far from the centre, where it does the most to resist bending, for very little weight.

parts.name: Right upper arm bone

parts.description: Rotary actuator that bends the right elbow, strong enough to lift a heavy box.

details.didYouKnow: A human biceps attaches only a few centimetres from the elbow, so it pulls with several times the weight in your hand; robot elbows avoid that leverage problem by putting the gearbox right on the joint.
details.howItWorks: Two angle sensors often sit in the elbow, one on the motor and one on the output, so the controller can see how much the gearbox and structure twist under load. keyNumbers: Angle sensors typically resolve tiny fractions of a degree
Commonly part of the 28 or more body actuators
Lifts loads of up to roughly 10 kg per arm near the body
details.madeOf: A brushless motor with a strain-wave or cycloidal gearbox and magnetic angle encoders in a cast aluminium housing. Magnetic encoders are compact and tolerate dust and vibration well.

parts.name: Right elbow actuator

parts.description: Forearm packed with the small motors that pull the fingers through cables, keeping the hand light.

details.didYouKnow: Carpal tunnel syndrome in people happens where finger tendons squeeze through the wrist, the same tight spot that gives robot designers the most trouble with friction.
details.howItWorks: Moving the motors into the forearm means the cables have to bend through the wrist, and they stretch slightly and rub as they go. Tendon cables usually well under 1 mm thick
Forearm and hand together roughly 2 to 3 kg

parts.name: Right forearm & hand motors

parts.description: Six small motors in the forearm, each winding a steel cable that runs through the wrist to curl one finger.

details.didYouKnow: This is exactly how your own hand is built: the main muscles that bend your fingers are in your forearm, and there are no muscles in the fingers themselves.

Hands usually have around 10 or more joints

parts.name: Right finger motors

parts.description: Palm with touch sensors and a thumb that can oppose the fingers to pinch and grip.

details.didYouKnow: Your fingertips are among the most sensitive spots on your body, with a very high density of touch receptors; matching that sensitivity is still one of the hardest problems in robotics.
details.howItWorks: Touch sensors under the palm and fingertip skin detect contact, pressure and sometimes slip, which cameras alone cannot see once the hand closes round an object. keyNumbers: Often a dozen or more touch sensing areas
Touch sensors read many times per second
Hand typically weighs well under 1 kg
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic or light metal palm with a soft silicone or rubber skin containing pressure-sensing elements. Soft skin both protects the sensors and spreads pressure, much like the fat pads in a human palm.

parts.name: Right hand

parts.description: Four jointed fingers, each curled by a tendon cable and straightened by a spring or second cable.

details.didYouKnow: Human fingers contain no muscles at all; they are moved entirely by tendons from muscles in the palm and forearm, exactly the trick robot hands copy.
details.howItWorks: The fingers are a little springy by design, so they can bend slightly when they hit something unexpected instead of breaking or crushing it. Each finger roughly 7 to 10 cm long
A whole robot hand typically grips with tens of newtons of force

parts.name: Right fingers

parts.description: Group of powerful actuators that swing, spread and twist the right leg.

details.didYouKnow: Early full-size humanoids that needed big forces at the hips and knees often used hydraulics; the switch to all-electric designs came as motors and batteries became powerful enough to match them.

Three actuators per hip
Supports up to about 20 kg of payload on top of the body

parts.name: Right hip strain-wave gear

parts.description: Long, stiff thigh link built to carry the robot's weight with every step.

details.didYouKnow: A leg swings like a pendulum, and putting the heavy parts high up makes it act like a shorter, faster pendulum, which is one reason long-legged animals have thin lower legs.
details.howItWorks: The thigh's length together with the shin's sets how long a stride can be and how high a step the robot can climb. Designers also try to keep its mass close to the hip, so the leg swings forwards quickly with little effort. Its surface is often shaped to leave room for the opposite leg's knee as the legs pass each other.

Thigh link weighs roughly 2 to 4 kg with its actuator

parts.name: Right knee push screw

parts.description: The robot's strongest joint, driven by a linear actuator, a screw that pushes like a muscle.

details.didYouKnow: The word robot was first used in the Czech play R.U.R. by Karel Capek in 1920, from 'robota', meaning forced labour; his robots were made of artificial flesh, not motors and screws.
details.howItWorks: Climbing stairs, standing up from a crouch and carrying loads all put the biggest demands on the knees, because the body's weight sits far from the joint when it is bent. That is why the knee is often the strongest actuator. Not every robot uses a screw: some use a large rotary actuator with a high-ratio gearbox at the joint, trading a bulkier knee for a simpler design.
keyNumbers: Human knees carry roughly 3 to 4 times body weight climbing stairs
Usually the single strongest joint in the robot

parts.name: Right knee actuator

parts.description: Lower leg link carrying the ankle actuators' push rods down to the foot.

details.didYouKnow: Falling safely is a skill robots have to learn too; controllers try to turn a fall into a crouch or roll so that tough parts like the shins and hips take the impact instead of the head or hands.
details.howItWorks: The shin takes the hardest knocks, from furniture, stairs and falls, so its cover acts partly as a guard. Inside, the ankle push rods run close to the main structure and are protected from impacts that could bend them. Joint sensors and cables for the foot's force sensors also pass through here.
keyNumbers: Typically about 35 to 45 cm long
Push rods often only about 1 cm thick
Each rod can carry forces of hundreds of newtons or more
details.madeOf: A tough plastic outer cover, sometimes with impact-absorbing padding, over an aluminium or composite tube. The cover is designed to be swapped cheaply if scuffed or cracked.

parts.name: Right shin

parts.description: Two steel rods that carry force from motors high in the shin down to the ankle, keeping weight away from the foot so the leg swings easily.

details.didYouKnow: Mass low on the leg is expensive because it is swung with every step, and that's why runners' calves taper to thin tendons at the ankle, the same design as here.
details.howItWorks: Motors mounted high in the shin push and pull these two rods. Moving them together tips the foot up and down; moving them opposite ways rocks it from side to side, so two motors share both jobs.
keyNumbers: Typically 25 to 30 cm long
Two degrees of freedom from two rods
Ankles commonly see more than body weight on each step
details.madeOf: Steel or titanium rods with ball joints at each end, and the motors kept far above the ankle.

parts.name: Right ankle push rods

parts.description: Pair of actuators that tip the foot up, down and sideways to keep balance on uneven ground.

details.didYouKnow: Your Achilles tendon stores energy like a spring with every stride and gives much of it back; many robot legs still waste that energy, which is one reason walking robots use more power than people.
details.howItWorks: Because the ankle actuators are springy and can be controlled softly, the foot can settle onto an uneven surface rather than landing rigidly and bouncing. The controller lowers the ankle's stiffness just as the foot touches down, then firms it up once weight is on it. That gentle landing stops shocks from rattling the cameras and computer above.
keyNumbers: Typically about 15 to 20 degrees of side-to-side tilt
Two actuators sharing the work
Stiffness adjusted within a few thousandths of a second at touchdown

parts.name: Right ankle actuators

parts.description: Flat foot with force sensors in the sole that feel where the robot's weight is pressing.

details.didYouKnow: A human foot has 26 bones and dozens of joints, while most robot feet are a single flat plate, which is one reason humanoids still struggle on loose sand and rocky trails.
details.howItWorks: Each step lands heel first in many controllers, rolls across the sole and pushes off from the front, spreading the impact and helping the robot walk more like a person. The rubber sole provides grip on smooth floors and soaks up small bumps. Sensors in the foot also tell the controller the moment of contact, which is the cue to shift weight onto this leg.

Rubber sole a few millimetres to about 1 cm thick
Touch-down detected within a few thousandths of a second

parts.name: Right foot

summary: A general-purpose humanoid robot: a human-shaped body of electric actuators at every joint, hands with tendon-driven fingers, a battery in the chest and an AI computer that turns camera images into movements.
